extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators and appellate attorneys (practitioners preparing or opposing appeals and certiorari in patent cases)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting a Supreme Court brief in opposition in a patent appeal that focuses on appealability, waiver, Rule 50 preservation, and patent-eligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101 (Alice). Emphasizes how to frame factual posture (effective grants of summary judgment) and discretionary doctrines to defeat certiorari.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice § 101 two-step test
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining patent-eligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101 requires a two-step inquiry: (1) decide whether the claims are directed to a traditional patent-ineligible concept (laws of nature, natural phenomena, or abstract ideas) (Alice Step One); and (2) if so, ask whether the remaining elements, alone or in combination, supply an "inventive concept" that "transforms the nature of the claim" into a patent-eligible application (Alice Step Two).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Alice, 573 U.S. 208, 217-218. Use Mayo/Alice lineage: if claims merely require a generic computer to perform generic functions, they fail Step Two. Include the Mayo language about "well-understood, routine, conventional activities previously known in the industry."

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice Step One — directed to an abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the claim as a whole is directed to an abstract idea (or other traditional exception). For example, the court found the asserted claims were directed to "the abstract idea of controlling access to, or limiting permission to, resources."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare claim language to precedent; consider whether multiple claim terms collapse into a single, abstract concept (e.g., several components collapsing into an access-controller concept). Do not rely on extrinsic facts if the claim language itself resolves the question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice Step Two — presence of an inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask whether the claim elements, individually or as an ordered combination, provide an inventive concept sufficient to transform an abstract idea into a patent-eligible application. Claims cannot survive Step Two if they recite only "well-understood, routine, conventional activities" or generic computer functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An alleged inventive feature must be part of the claims (not only in the specification). Unclaimed or merely described features (e.g., a 'layered architecture' in the specification but not claimed) cannot be relied on to supply an inventive concept. Cite Berkheimer where factual disputes about whether elements are "well-understood, routine, conventional" may preclude summary judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-understood, routine, conventional activities test
rubrics_metrics.description: To defeat Step Two, a court asks whether the claimed additional elements are well-understood, routine, and conventional activities previously known in the industry (Mayo/Alice language).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If resolution of whether elements are routine is fact-dependent (per Berkheimer), summary judgment may be inappropriate; conversely, if the record and claim language show only generic functionality, summary judgment is proper. Use factual record only when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purely legal determination vs. factual dispute
rubrics_metrics.description: A determination that rests solely on the 'four corners' of the patent (the patent as a legal document) and does not rely on any historical facts—disputed or undisputed—is a purely legal question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a § 101 ruling is confined to the patent text and precedent, it is a legal determination suitable for summary judgment and appeal. Emphasize patents are legal documents (citing Goodyear, Motion Picture Patents) to support characterization as law rather than fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectively granted summary judgment (denial that is an effective grant)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a district court 'denies' a movant's summary-judgment motion but, in substance, decides the issue for the nonmovant (leaving nothing for the jury), that denial is treated as an 'effective grant' (or sua sponte grant) of summary judgment in favor of the nonmovant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts treat such rulings like an express grant of summary judgment and permit appeals from them. Cite cases (e.g., Lighting Ballast, Hudson, National Elec. Mfrs.) showing multiple circuits equate effective grants with appealable grants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appealability of summary-judgment grants without Rule 50
rubrics_metrics.description: All circuits permit appeals from grants of summary judgment without first proceeding through Rule 50, because Rule 50 applies only when a party has been 'fully heard on an issue during a jury trial.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the issue was resolved pre-trial by summary judgment (or an effective grant), Rule 50 cannot and need not be invoked. Collect circuit precedent (First through Federal Circuit) that reviews appeals from summary-judgment orders even where the case went to trial on other issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 50 trigger and preservation requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 50 applies only if a party has been 'fully heard on an issue during a jury trial' (Rule 50(a)); Rule 50(b) requires issues to have first been presented under Rule 50(a) before being raised post-trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an issue did not proceed to trial because it was resolved on summary judgment (or effectively so), a Rule 50(a) motion could not have been made and Rule 50 preservation is inapplicable. Emphasize textual rule limits to counter waiver arguments based on Rule 50.

rubrics_metrics.name: When summary-judgment denials require Rule 50 preservation
rubrics_metrics.description: If a summary-judgment motion is denied because factual disputes remain for trial (e.g., under Berkheimer), then Rule 50 and related post-trial motions may be necessary to preserve specific arguments for appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish denials that leave factual issues for the jury (which may require Rule 50 preservation) from denials that effectively decide a pure legal issue (which do not). Use district-court posture to show whether facts remained for trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate discretion to excuse waiver
rubrics_metrics.description: Appellate courts have discretion to excuse a party's waiver of an argument and consider it on appeal when appropriate; this is a discretionary doctrine without a general limiting rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors supporting excusing waiver include: the issue was fully presented and briefed in district court; deciding the issue on appeal would not prejudice either party; remand would serve no purpose; declining review would result in manifest injustice; or the proper resolution is beyond doubt. Cite Singleton, Exxon Shipping, Automated Merch. Sys., Fabri, and related authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction and reliance on unclaimed/specification-only features
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventive-concept argument must be grounded in claim language or a correct claim construction; relying on features present only in the specification (unclaimed features) is improper to establish patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a party wants to limit or supply an inventive feature (e.g., 'layered architecture'), it should propose that limitation during claim construction; courts will not import unclaimed features post hoc to save claims under § 101.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using trial testimony on appeal to show inconsistent litigation positions
rubrics_metrics.description: Appellate courts may reference trial testimony to demonstrate that a party's trial positions contradicted positions asserted earlier (e.g., at summary judgment), but reliance on such testimony does not imply the § 101 issue was not decided at summary judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use trial record to highlight contradictions as a tactical point; clarify that the dispositive legal ruling was confined to the patent's text so appellate review remains appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circuit precedent analysis on appealability
rubrics_metrics.description: When arguing appealability, analyze and cite regional-circuit decisions showing uniform permission to appeal in situations where summary-judgment rulings are effectively grants or pure legal determinations; show that perceived 'circuit split' disappears when the district-court ruling is properly characterized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematically address each circuit's cases (First through Federal Circuit) and distinguish full denials based on factual issues from effective grants/pure legal rulings. Use multiple circuit citations (CMM Cable, Barkley, Owatanna, Brown, Lighting Ballast, etc.) to demonstrate consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prejudice, remand purpose, and manifest injustice considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: When deciding whether to excuse waiver or to exercise appellate jurisdiction, courts weigh whether appellate review will prejudice the nonmovant, whether remand would serve any purpose, and whether refusal to review would produce manifest injustice (e.g., allowing collection on an invalid patent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame arguments to show lack of prejudice (the issue was fully litigated), futility of remand (issue resolved purely as a matter of law), and risk of manifest injustice to justify appellate intervention and defeat certiorari.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterizing patents as legal instruments for legal questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents are legal documents (like contracts or deeds); when the § 101 inquiry can be resolved by interpreting the patent text against controlling law, the question is legal rather than factual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Goodyear Dental Vulcanite Co. v. Davis and Motion Picture Patents Co. to support arguing that patent-text-based decisions fit within appellate reviewable legal issues and are thus appealable without Rule 50 preservation.
